# Alpha-OSK

> A free, open-source assistive on-screen keyboard for Windows and Linux, with
> word prediction that learns on the user's own machine. Built for people who
> cannot comfortably use a physical keyboard but can move a cursor.

Alpha-OSK is a desktop application. The user clicks keys in a floating keyboard
window and the keystrokes are delivered to whichever application currently has
operating-system focus. The keyboard never takes focus itself.

Unlike other on-screen keyboards, it uses both mouse buttons. Right-clicking a
character key types its shifted variant, a modifier key locks it held, a
prediction pill opens a menu to correct the word model, a function key opens an
editor to bind a shortcut or a phrase to it, a snippet tile opens its actions,
and the title bar opens a window menu. Every one of those actions also has a
left-click route, for pointers driven by dwell-clicking, eye trackers or
switches, which have no second button.

Prediction merges an n-gram model of the user's own vocabulary with a spatial
model of the keys surrounding the one actually clicked, so a mis-clicked key is
still completed to the intended word. There is no large language model and no
GPU requirement, and the model never leaves the machine.

Key facts:

- Licence: MIT. Free for personal and commercial use. No account, no subscription.
- Platforms: Windows 10/11 (EV-signed installer, auto-updating) and Linux
  (AppImage, requires xdotool on X11 or ydotool on Wayland). macOS is in
  progress and not released.
- Privacy: learning is entirely on-device. Password fields pause learning
  automatically. Two features transmit anything at all, both off by default and
  both opt-in: voice dictation, which requires the user's own Deepgram API key
  and sends audio only while the microphone is open; and anonymous usage stats,
  which send nine integer counters a week, never content, word frequencies, key
  frequencies, IP or hostname.
- Measured savings: the opt-in counters are summed across installs and appended
  to a public dated CSV once a day, and the current row is what the figures on
  the home page are read from. Separately, a replayed benchmark on a corpus of
  AAC-like communications puts the prediction engine at 49 to 50% keystroke
  savings; the white paper describes that as an upper bound under an idealised
  user rather than an estimate of real-world benefit, and notes there is no user
  study.
- Author: Owen Kent, a wheelchair user with muscular dystrophy who uses the
  keyboard daily to develop it.
